scope: Original shared mathematical supplements. Inventory every stated assumption and substantive proof move, identify prerequisites and omissions from natural mathematics before opening any Lean/reconstruction packet. This is not a source fidelity verdict.

units.title: Continuous weights from dyadic prefix limits
units.statement: Suppose signed cell masses along a cofinal sequence of dyadic levels have uniformly bounded total absolute mass. If their prefix sums at each fixed dyadic node converge to the prefix integral of an integrable time density, the left-endpoint sum against any continuous weight converges to the integral of the weighted density.
assumptions: The horizon T is positive and the sequence of fine levels tends to infinity.
The real weight w is continuous on [0,T], and the real density b is integrable against the horizon time measure.
The total absolute cell mass is uniformly bounded along the specified sequence. For every fixed dyadic node, the inclusive fine prefix converges to the integral primitive of b at that node.

proof.title: Freeze the weights on a coarse grid
proof.text: Hold the coarse level m fixed. Once the fine level σ(n) is at least m, use the coarse left-endpoint weight for every fine cell it contains. The block identity and the prefix hypotheses give the limit as a finite sum of weighted primitive differences.

proof.title: Bound the freezing error
proof.text: For these refining fine levels, each fine left endpoint and its coarse left endpoint are in the same coarse cell. Uniform continuity on [0,T] bounds the difference of the two weights. Multiply that bound by the uniform bound on total absolute mass.

proof.title: Pass to the weighted integral
proof.text: The existing deterministic weighted time-sum theorem gives the limit of Lₘ. Choose m so both the freezing error and the error in Lₘ are small, then take the fine level sufficiently large.

units.boundary: The cell masses may be signed. Bounded total absolute mass along the sequence is the condition used to control the uniform weight error.

units.title: Continuous-weight covariation of two completed Itô rows
units.statement: Let X and Y be two real Itô rows driven by the same standard vector Brownian motion relative to the given filtration and measure. For an almost surely continuous real weight with measurable time slices, the left-endpoint weighted products of dyadic increments converge in measure to the time integral of the weight times the inner product of the diffusion coefficients.
assumptions: The horizon T is positive. The sample measure is finite, and the filtration satisfies the usual conditions. The coordinate set is finite with decidable equality.

Each row uses progressive square-integrable coefficients on the product of the sample measure and the horizon time measure. Its drift has almost-everywhere strongly measurable evaluations up to T and almost surely continuous finite-variation paths on [0,T].
At each fixed t≤T the weight W(t) is almost-everywhere strongly measurable. Almost every weight path is continuous on [0,T].

notation.text: Each real row uses the corresponding scalar stochastic integral against every coordinate of the same Brownian motion.

proof.title: Choose a common subsequence of actual limits
proof.text: On any subsequence, apply the countable selection theorem to all mixed prefix limits and the two terminal square-sum limits. This gives a further subsequence on which the limits hold together almost everywhere.

proof.title: Control the signed cell masses
proof.text: The absolute product of the two increments is bounded by half their squared sum. The two terminal limits bound this sum along the selected subsequence. The coefficient products have integrable time sections by product L² and Fubini.

proof.title: Apply the continuous-weight limit pathwise
proof.text: For almost every sample, the continuous weight, the bounded signed masses, and the cumulative limits satisfy the deterministic theorem. Apply the subsequence characterization of convergence in measure.
proof.formula: S_{n_\ell}\to\int W(s)\sum_j\eta_j(s)\xi_j(s)\,ds\quad\text{almost everywhere along the selected subsequence}.

units.boundary: The limit is for the full horizon and is in measure. The weight assumptions suffice for this quadratic term. The first-order stochastic integral and the full smooth Itô identity have their own contracts.

units.title: Covariation of two Itô rows up to a fixed dyadic time
units.statement: Let X and Y be two real Itô rows driven by the same finite-dimensional Brownian motion. Fix a coarse dyadic time τ. The sum of products of the increments of X and Y over fine cells ending at or before τ converges in measure to the time integral of the inner product of their diffusion rows up to τ.
assumptions: The underlying measure is finite. The filtration satisfies the usual conditions, and B is a standard Euclidean Brownian motion relative to that filtration and measure.

The two finite rows of coefficients η and ξ are progressive and square-integrable for the product of the horizon time measure and the underlying measure. The Brownian coordinate index set has decidable equality.
The drift evaluations of X and Y are almost-everywhere strongly measurable at every deterministic time t≤T. Almost every drift path is continuous and has bounded variation on [0,T].
The horizon T is positive. The fixed cutoff τ is any coarse dyadic grid point, including the endpoints.

notation.text: Each row includes its own drift and one completed scalar Itô integral per Brownian coordinate.
At level n the fine grid has 2ⁿ cells. The cutoff belongs to a fixed coarse grid.

proof.title: Form the sum of the two rows
proof.text: The sum of the drifts is continuous with variation at most the sum of the two variations. The integrands add in progressive L². Linearity of the completed Itô integral identifies the summed row Z with X+Y almost everywhere at each fine-grid time.

proof.title: Polarize the three scalar limits
proof.text: Apply the scalar prefix theorem to Z, X and Y. The cell identity below turns the mixed increment sum into half the difference of their square sums. From any subsequence, extract a further one on which all three square sums converge almost everywhere and take the same linear combination there.

proof.title: Identify the limit on each Brownian coordinate
proof.text: Each of the three squared coefficients is integrable in time on almost every path by product L² and Fubini. Apply the same polarization identity inside the restricted time integrals and sum over the coordinates.

units.boundary: The cutoff is fixed and the limit is in measure. Varying weights and pathwise or uniform-in-time convergence have separate contracts.

units.title: Read the time energy of a step process
units.statement: For a fixed sample path, the real time integral of an elementary adapted process squared equals the sum of its squared coefficients weighted by the lengths of its cells clipped at T.
assumptions: An elementary adapted real process on a finite strictly increasing grid, with its stored left-endpoint measurable bounded coefficients.
Any nonnegative horizon T and any sample point ω. The clipped interval lengths are nonnegative.

proof.title: Evaluate the nonnegative integral
proof.text: The existing cell formula evaluates the nonnegative Lebesgue integral. The squared coefficients and clipped lengths are finite, so the formula is a finite sum of finite terms. Convert the nonnegative integral to ℝ to obtain the real integral.

units.boundary: The equality is pointwise in the sample, including when T cuts a cell or no cell lies before T.

units.title: Quadratic variation up to a common stop
units.statement: Evaluate the original finite Itô row at a common bounded stopping time capped by the evaluation time. The dyadic squared-increment sum of this stopped row converges in L¹ to the original square energy accumulated up to that stop, with integrable signed error at every level.
assumptions: One Euclidean Brownian motion under the sample measure μ, relative to the given filtration. The coordinates in a finite index set J come from this same motion.
The sample measure is finite. The horizon T is positive and the filtration satisfies the usual conditions.
Each coordinate input is progressive and product-space square integrable. One finite-valued stopping time τ is shared by all coordinates and satisfies 0 ≤ τ(ω) ≤ T at every sample point.

proof.title: Identify the stopped row at every grid endpoint
proof.text: Use the fixed-time stopping theorem at all endpoints of one finite grid. This identifies the actual stopped row with the completed row of closed stopped integrands almost surely.

proof.title: Identify the stopped energy
proof.text: Squaring the stopped integrand preserves its indicator. Integrate the original coefficient squared on the closed interval ending at τ.

proof.title: Apply the progressive-row theorem
proof.text: Stopping preserves progressive L². Replace the row values and energy at each level by their identified counterparts and use the already proved L¹ limit.

units.boundary: The grid is deterministic. The single common stop is random and is applied to every row evaluation.

units.title: A progressive integrand for a sphere noise coordinate
units.statement: Evaluate a projected Brownian column along a progressively measurable sphere-valued process. With continuous deterministic temperature, the scalar coefficient defines a strongly progressive $L^2$ integrand on every finite horizon.
assumptions: The sample measure is finite. The filtration is indexed by nonnegative time. $I$ is finite and has decidable equality.
The process takes values in the Euclidean unit sphere. It is jointly measurable and strongly progressive. The deterministic temperature is continuous.

The horizon is nonnegative. The real square root is the total Lean operation. The defining coefficient formula holds at every nonnegative time, and the product $L^2$ property uses the specified finite horizon.

proof.title: Build a jointly continuous scalar coefficient
proof.text: Take the coordinate of the projected vector and multiply by the square root of twice the temperature. The coordinate maps and the total real square root are continuous.

proof.title: Use compactness on the horizon
proof.text: The unit sphere is compact. The continuous-coefficient lemma gives strong progressiveness and product-space square integrability with the chosen horizon measure.

units.boundary: The product-space condition is specific to the chosen horizon. The coefficient is defined on the full nonnegative time axis.

units.title: The projected noise representative has the literal coefficient
units.statement: For the constructed finite-horizon sphere integrand, the process value is exactly the projected scalar coefficient at every nonnegative time and every sample.
assumptions: The sample measure is finite. The filtration is indexed by nonnegative time. $I$ is finite and has decidable equality.
The process takes values in the Euclidean unit sphere. It is jointly measurable and strongly progressive. The deterministic temperature is continuous.

The horizon is nonnegative. The real square root is the total Lean operation. The defining coefficient formula holds at every nonnegative time, and the product $L^2$ property uses the specified finite horizon.

proof.title: Read the process field of the integrand
proof.text: The integrand construction stores the original scalar function as its representative. Taking the process field recovers that function pointwise.

units.boundary: The literal representative is exposed on the full time axis. Integrability is on the selected horizon.

units.title: The canonical sphere coordinate equation gives the weak evolution
units.statement: For a sphere-valued process satisfying the displayed integrated coordinate equations, the derivative of every smooth test expectation equals the expected sphere generator. It is the ordinary derivative at positive times and the right derivative at zero.
assumptions: The probability space has a filtration and standard Euclidean Brownian motion relative to it, with the usual conditions. The Euclidean coordinate set is finite with decidable equality.

The sphere-valued process is jointly measurable and strongly progressive, with almost surely continuous paths. The ambient field is jointly continuous, and the deterministic temperature is continuous and nonnegative.

For every positive horizon the stated integrated equation holds on one full-measure event for all times in that horizon and all coordinates. It uses the literal drift and the constructed completed Brownian integrals.
The real ambient test is twice continuously differentiable at every sphere point.

proof.title: Use the actual coordinate equation
proof.text: Strong progressiveness gives time-zero measurability of the initial coordinates. Continuity and compactness prove progressiveness and integrability of the scalar drift. The noise integrands have the literal projected coefficients.

proof.title: Apply the weak evolution for the assembled rows
proof.text: The path equation identifies the assembled vector with the supplied sphere process on the common horizon event. The existing sphere-row theorem gives the expected generator as the derivative.

units.boundary: The coordinate equation is the supplied process input. The conclusion gives the evolution of test expectations for that process.

units.title: A time primitive has bounded variation
units.statement: The prefix integral of an integrable real time density has finite variation on the closed horizon.
assumptions: The horizon T is nonnegative. The real density b is integrable against nonnegative time measure restricted to [0,T].

proof.title: Control one increment
proof.text: A prefix increment is the integral of b over one time cell. Its absolute value is bounded by the integral of |b| over the same cell.

proof.title: Telescope the bound
proof.text: Sum the bounds on any finite nondecreasing list of times in the horizon. The absolute-density prefixes telescope, and the final prefix is finite.

units.boundary: The Lean conclusion records bounded variation. The proof establishes the displayed quantitative bound, including T=0.

units.title: Left-weighted sums of completed Itô increments
units.statement: The dyadic sums of the original completed scalar Itô increments, weighted at left endpoints, converge in measure to the completed terminal integral of the literal product of the weight and the original input.
assumptions: There is one scalar Brownian motion relative to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions, a finite sample measure μ, and a positive deterministic horizon T.
The input η is real, progressive and product-space L². The weight is strongly progressive globally, almost surely continuous on [0,T], and uniformly bounded pointwise for t∈[0,T].

proof.title: Construct the literal product
proof.text: Strong progressiveness is closed under multiplication. The product time measure is supported on [0,T], so the horizon bound suffices for square integrability of the global literal product.

proof.title: Assemble the single-cell integrals
proof.text: Each left value is strongly measurable in its left filtration and bounded. The single-cell multiplier identity converts the weighted increment to a completed integral on that cell. Add the finite family.

proof.title: Pass to the product integral
proof.text: Left samples converge along continuous paths. Their squared product errors are dominated by a constant times |η|². The terminal Itô isometry carries product L² convergence to convergence in measure of the actual terminal processes.
proof.formula: w_n\eta\to w\eta\text{ in product }L^2,\qquad I_T(w_n\eta)\to I_T(w\eta)\text{ in measure}.

units.boundary: The conclusion is convergence in measure to the actual completed integral on the same Brownian driver.

units.title: Differentiate a projected coordinate field
units.statement: For any coordinate j, ambient base point x and direction u, the Fréchet derivative of the field σ_j applied to u is −(x_j u+u_j x).
assumptions: I is a finite coordinate type with decidable equality. The space is real Euclidean space on I.
Write e_j for the j-th coordinate vector and σ_j(x)=e_j−x_j x.
Both x and u are arbitrary ambient vectors.

proof.title: Differentiate the scalar and vector factors
proof.text: The coordinate functional has derivative u↦u_j and the identity has derivative u↦u. The fixed coordinate vector has derivative zero.

units.boundary: This is the ambient derivative of the quadratic field.

units.title: Finite sums preserve convergence in measure
units.statement: On a finite measure space, take a finite family of sequences of almost-everywhere strongly measurable functions into a seminormed additive commutative group. If each sequence converges in measure to its given limit, the sums converge in measure to the sum of the limits.
assumptions: The index set is finite and the sample measure is finite. The codomain is a seminormed additive commutative group.
Each term is almost-everywhere strongly measurable. Each sequence converges in measure to its given limit.

proof.title: Use one subsequence for the whole family
proof.text: Start from any subsequence and choose a single further subsequence on which all component limits hold almost everywhere.
proof.formula: F_{i,n_{k_\ell}}(\omega)\to G_i(\omega)\qquad\text{for every }i\text{ on one full-measure event}.

proof.title: Sum the limits
proof.text: Continuity of finite addition gives the sum limit on that event. The finite sums are almost-everywhere strongly measurable, so the subsequence criterion gives convergence in measure.

units.boundary: This result concerns finite sums. Infinite sums require additional convergence control.

units.title: Expand a Euclidean bilinear form in coordinates
units.statement: Let H be a continuous real bilinear form on a finite-dimensional Euclidean coordinate space. Evaluating H on vectors x and y gives the sum over ordered coordinate pairs of their coordinates multiplied by the corresponding basis entry.
assumptions: The coordinate type is finite with decidable equality. The vectors eᵢ are the standard Euclidean orthonormal basis.
H is linear in each argument and continuous. The vectors x and y are arbitrary.

proof.title: Use the underlying bilinear map
proof.text: Forget continuity in each of the two linear maps. This keeps every evaluation equal.

proof.title: Apply the basis expansion
proof.text: The algebraic bilinear basis theorem expands both arguments. In the standard Euclidean basis the representation coefficients are the actual coordinates.

units.boundary: The expansion works for every continuous bilinear form. Symmetry and positive semidefiniteness play no role.

units.title: Measurable slices and continuous paths of completed Euclidean Itô rows
units.statement: Construct a finite-dimensional Euclidean process from scalar completed Itô rows with almost surely continuous drift paths. Every slice up to the horizon is measurable, and almost every vector path is continuous on the horizon.
assumptions: The positive horizon is T. The sample measure is finite, the filtration satisfies the usual conditions, and the driving standard vector Brownian motion is relative to that filtration and measure.
The finite coordinate rows have progressive product-square-integrable diffusion coefficients. Their drift evaluations at each fixed time t≤T are almost-everywhere strongly measurable.
Each drift coordinate is continuous on [0,T] almost surely.
units.formula: X_t^i=A_i(t)+\sum_j\int_0^t\eta_{ij}(s)\,dB^j_s.\qquad X_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R^I\text{ measurable for each }t\le T,\quad X_\cdot(\omega)\text{ continuous on }[0,T]\text{ a.e.}

proof.title: Assemble measurable slices
proof.text: Strong adaptation gives measurable slices of each completed integral. A finite sum with the drift is almost-everywhere strongly measurable. Completeness from the usual conditions gives ordinary measurability of that slice.

proof.title: Assemble continuous paths
proof.text: The completed integrals have continuous paths on the horizon. Intersect the finitely many drift continuity events and use continuity of each coordinate to get continuity in the Euclidean topology.
proof.formula: \bigl(\forall i,\ X_\cdot^i(\omega)\text{ continuous on }[0,T]\bigr)\Longrightarrow X_\cdot(\omega)\text{ continuous on }[0,T].

units.boundary: Only continuity and measurable slices on the horizon are asserted. The drift path hypothesis is continuity.

units.title: Weighted mixed products of Brownian increments
units.statement: For distinct coordinates of the same Euclidean Brownian motion, the predictably weighted sum of their simultaneous increment products vanishes in mean square on dyadic grids.
assumptions: One Euclidean Brownian driver and its given filtration.
Distinct coordinates and square-integrable weights measurable at each left endpoint.
One uniform second-moment bound on the weights. T may be zero.

proof.title: Read the mean-square conclusion of the mixed-increment theorem
proof.text: The preceding theorem proves both square integrability at each dyadic level and the asserted vanishing second moment. Select its second conclusion; no extra moment or independence assumption is introduced.

units.boundary: Mean-square control of the literal mixed increment sum for the specified grid weights.

units.title: Terminal Itô formula for sphere-valued integrated rows
units.statement: For the initialized row process $X$ specified below, the generator is $\mathcal L_t f(X_t)$ with field value $u_t$ at the sample. There exists a real martingale $M$ for the given filtration with $M_0(\omega)=0$ at every sample, and the terminal increment has the displayed almost-sure decomposition.
assumptions: The sample measure is finite. A standard Euclidean Brownian motion is given relative to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions. The finite coordinate set $I$ has decidable equality and the horizon $T$ is strictly positive.

Each initialized row is $x_i+\int_0^t b_i(s)\,ds+\sum_j\int_0^t\eta_{ij}(s)\,dB_j(s)$ using the library's completed stochastic integral on that horizon. The initial coordinates are strongly measurable in $\mathcal F_0$. Each drift coordinate is strongly progressive with an integrable time section almost surely. Each noise entry is a strongly progressive product-space $L^2$ integrand.

On full-measure horizon events, the row process stays on the unit sphere at every $t\le T$ and the coefficients are $b(t)=-u_t-\lambda(t)(|I|-1)X_t$ and $\sigma_j(t)=\sqrt{2\lambda(t)}P_{X_t}e_j$ at all such times and all $j$. Here $P_we_j=e_j-w_jw$.
The real deterministic temperature is pointwise nonnegative up to $T$. The ambient test is $C^2$ at every sphere point, and a sphere point is supplied for the compact-range construction.
The ambient sphere Laplacian is $\Delta_S^{\mathrm{ext}}f(w)=\sum_j D^2f(w)[P_we_j,P_we_j]-(|I|-1)Df(w)[w]$.

proof.title: Apply Itô to the integrated rows
proof.text: The existing compact-range Itô formula gives a first-order term, the quadratic term with factor one half, and a zero-start martingale.
proof.detail: Obtain the initialized drift regularity and apply the compact Euclidean formula.

proof.title: Add the drift and Hessian integrals
proof.text: The row integrability theorem makes both terms integrable on the same almost-sure horizon event. The projected column identity combines their integrands.

units.boundary: The integrated Brownian row process and its almost-sure sphere range are inputs. The conclusion concerns the terminal horizon.

units.title: Weak marginal evolution from sphere diffusion rows
units.statement: Use the actual laws $\rho_t=(X_t)_\#P$. Put $F(t)=\int f(w)\,d\rho_{t^+}(w)$ and $B(t)=\int\mathcal L_{t^+}f(w)\,d\rho_{t^+}(w)$. The generator average $B$ is locally integrable on the real line. The expectation $F$ is absolutely continuous on each finite nonnegative interval and has the signed two-time balance and almost-everywhere derivative below.
assumptions: The sample space carries a probability measure $P$, a filtration indexed by nonnegative real time satisfying the usual conditions, and a standard Euclidean Brownian motion relative to that filtration. The coordinate set $I$ is finite with decidable equality.
The process $X$ is jointly measurable and takes values in the Euclidean unit sphere $S$. The field $u(t,w)$ is jointly continuous and ambient-vector-valued.
The deterministic temperature $\lambda$ is Borel measurable, nonnegative at each time, and bounded pointwise on each finite horizon. The ambient real test $f$ is $C^2$ at every point of $S$.

For each strictly positive horizon, supply initialized coordinates strongly measurable in $\mathcal F_0$, strongly progressive drift rows with almost-sure integrable sections, and strongly progressive product-$L^2$ noise rows. Their initialized integral equation agrees with $X$ almost surely simultaneously for all horizon times. On the corresponding full-measure events the drift is $-u(t,X_t)-\lambda(t)(|I|-1)X_t$ and each noise column is $\sqrt{2\lambda(t)}P_{X_t}e_j$ throughout the horizon.
Here $P_we_j=e_j-w_jw$ and $t^+=\max(t,0)$. Both endpoints in the signed balance are arbitrary nonnegative times.
The sphere generator is $\mathcal L_t f(w)=-Df(w)[u(t,w)]+\lambda(t)\Delta_S^{\mathrm{ext}}f(w)$, with $\Delta_S^{\mathrm{ext}}f(w)=\sum_j D^2f(w)[P_we_j,P_we_j]-(|I|-1)Df(w)[w]$.

proof.title: Bound the generator on compact horizons
proof.text: The derivative weights and continuous field give uniform bounds on the compact state and time sets. Multiply the Laplacian bound by the horizon bound for the Borel temperature.
proof.detail: Use continuity of the derivative restrictions and the bound on temperature.

proof.title: Center the terminal increment
proof.text: The horizon-specific rows satisfy the sphere Itô formula. The martingale has expectation zero at the terminal time because it starts at zero. Convert the restricted nonnegative time integral into the real interval integral.

proof.title: Use the marginal balance theorem
proof.text: The centered increment applies at each terminal time. At time zero the increment and integral are both zero. The general marginal theorem gives the stated regularity and balance.

units.boundary: The integrated equations are assumptions on an existing process. The conclusion concerns the test expectations of its marginals.

units.title: Pointwise value of the projected noise representative
units.statement: The process field of the constructed integrand evaluates to the displayed coordinate at every nonnegative time and every sample.
assumptions: The filtration is indexed by nonnegative real time. The sample measure is finite, and the coordinate set $I$ is finite with decidable equality.
The process $X$ takes values in the Euclidean unit sphere, is jointly measurable for the product of the time Borel and sample measurable structures, and is strongly progressive.

For the selected horizon $T\ge0$, the real deterministic temperature is Borel measurable on nonnegative time and bounded in absolute value pointwise on $[0,T]$. The square root is the total real square root.
The symbol $\ell_T$ denotes Lebesgue time restricted to $[0,T]$. The $L^2$ membership uses $\mu\otimes\ell_T$, in sample-first order.

proof.title: Read the stored process field
proof.text: The construction stores the scalar function in the process field. Its integrability and progressiveness fields leave its pointwise value as displayed.
proof.detail: Unfold sphereMeasurableNoiseIntegrand and reduce the process projection.

units.boundary: The pointwise identity applies outside the selected horizon as well.

units.title: The second-order Taylor residual
units.statement: For any map f:E→F and points x,v∈E, define the residual after removing the constant, linear and quadratic terms by the displayed formula.
assumptions: Let E and F be real normed vector spaces. Derivatives are real Fréchet derivatives; D²f(x) is viewed as a continuous bilinear map.

proof.title: Subtract the quadratic Taylor polynomial
proof.text: This is a literal algebraic definition. Its use as a small error requires differentiability; the definition itself is total for every f.

units.boundary: This definition alone gives no estimate. Lean uses its total Fréchet-derivative convention when differentiability is absent.

units.title: A Hessian oscillation bound controls the Taylor residual
units.statement: If f is C² at every point of the segment from x to x+v and its Hessian differs there from D²f(x) in operator norm by at most ε, then the Taylor residual has norm at most ε‖v‖².
assumptions: Let E and F be real normed vector spaces. Derivatives are real Fréchet derivatives; D²f(x) is viewed as a continuous bilinear map.
For every t∈[0,1], f is C² at x+tv and ‖D²f(x+tv)−D²f(x)‖≤ε. The constant ε is real; these assumptions imply ε≥0.

proof.title: Differentiate along the segment
proof.text: After subtracting the first derivative and the Hessian at x, the derivative of the first-order error is exactly the Hessian variation applied twice to v.

proof.title: Bound the first-order error
proof.text: The operator-norm bound controls D′. Since D(0)=0, the mean-value inequality on the unit interval bounds D by the same constant.

proof.title: Apply the mean-value inequality a second time
proof.text: The residual along the segment has derivative D and starts at zero. Evaluating its bound at t=1 gives the conclusion.

units.boundary: The constant is an upper bound; no optimal factor of one half is asserted.

units.title: Dyadic predictable Brownian square errors vanish in mean square
units.statement: For the dyadic grids on [0,T], suppose all predictable weights have second moments bounded by one constant C, uniformly over levels and cells. Their compensated weighted square-increment sums tend to zero in mean square.
assumptions: B is a real Brownian motion with the given filtration and measure. The horizon T is any nonnegative real.
At every level n and cell i, the real weight is strongly measurable at time iT/2ⁿ and is in L². A real C satisfies E[aₙ,ᵢ²]≤C for every n,i.

proof.title: Apply the exact finite-grid identity
proof.text: Bound each diagonal weight moment by C and sum the equal cell lengths.

proof.title: Let the mesh tend to zero
proof.text: The upper bound tends to zero and the integrand is nonnegative, so the squeeze theorem gives the limit.

units.boundary: This is mean-square convergence of a centered error, not an almost-sure convergence assertion. It includes T=0.

units.title: Choose a representative with values in a specified set
units.statement: Define r:E→K by keeping each point already in K and replacing every point outside K by the specified fallback k₀.
assumptions: E is a type, K⊆E, and k₀ is a specified member of K. The result does not assume compactness.

proof.title: Use membership to choose the subtype value
proof.text: The first branch retains x with its membership proof; the second uses the given element of K.

units.boundary: The off-set fallback is an explicit part of this representative, not a projection or retraction supplied by geometry. For an almost-sure K-valued random variable, the change occurs only on its exceptional set.

units.title: Vanishing Taylor residuals on arbitrary fine grids
units.statement: On any compact pseudometric time space, take finite grids whose neighboring time distances vanish uniformly. If the sums of squared state increments converge in measure to a real-valued random variable Q, then the sums of second-order Taylor residuals converge in measure to zero.
assumptions: The sample space Ω carries a finite measure μ. E is a locally compact real normed space with its Borel measurable structure. K⊆E is compact.
f:E→ℝ is C² at every point of K. Each time evaluation of the K-valued process X is measurable. Its paths are continuous on the specified compact time domain for μ-almost every sample.

The time space is compact and pseudometric. Each grid has Nₙ+1 points, and for every δ>0, eventually all neighboring time distances are less than δ. Q:Ω→ℝ is a finite real-valued function. No ordering of the time space is required.

proof.title: Establish measurability of the residual sums
proof.text: The restrictions of f, Df and D²f to K are continuous. Hence the residual as a function of two K-valued endpoints is continuous, and the finite random sums are measurable.

proof.title: Extract a pathwise convergent energy subsequence
proof.text: From any subsequence, convergence in measure provides a further subsequence on which the square-increment sum converges almost everywhere. On each such continuous path it is eventually bounded by C=|Q|+1.

proof.title: Combine small increments with the uniform Taylor estimate
proof.text: Uniform continuity of each path turns the time-mesh condition into small state increments. Apply the compact uniform residual estimate with tolerance ε/(2C). The residual sum is then bounded by ε/2. The subsequence characterization yields convergence in measure.

units.boundary: Convergence of square-increment sums is an explicit input to this reusable lemma; the downstream Itô theorem derives it for its actual process. No rate or almost-sure limit for the full sequence is asserted.
